title: A slow gold through the moss

events.text: I am painting a banana slug crossing damp bark beneath a fern, inspired by the NPS forest-floor guide: https://www.nps.gov/redw/learn/nature/banana-slug-and-millipede.htm . Goal: a joined tapering gold body, unequal feeler curves, and one compact wet highlight. I will judge color coverage separately from raised relief.
Four washes leave pale linen lanes. I will bridge those gaps before placing the warm bark diagonal.
The bridge washes closed the linen lanes; horizontal bands remain. A broad bark diagonal will give the gold body a darker support.
The bark is joined and strongly ridged. I will build the slug from broad overlapping gold passes, tapering the left tail instead of drawing an outline.
The body is solid, with a tapered left tail and regular ridges. I will lift the head slightly and make the two long feelers unequal.
The head joins the body and the long feelers curve differently; the centered close view crops their tips. I will add smaller feelers and a restrained underside, then inspect the head directly.
The lower edge is darker without a full outline. I will separate the mantle from the tail with a broad warm plane, then add two small dark feeler tips.
The mantle is lighter than the tail and the tiny tips remain restrained. I will give the bark unequal cracks and a few moss cushions, avoiding the gold silhouette.
The cracks are quiet at whole view. A fern in the upper left will balance the rightward feelers; its stem should bend rather than form a straight ladder.
The fern is sparse and its lower leaf crosses the stem. I will fill the open intervals with unequal leaflets, keeping the central gold body unobstructed.
The fern leaflets read as narrow ribbons. I will broaden their bellies and attach the small upper tip rather than outlining each leaflet.
Broader leaflet bellies joined, though ribbon turns remain. I will vary the moss into shorter cushions and add a fallen leaf below the log.
The fallen leaf is still a strip. I will fill a broader folded shape and add a quiet mantle seam, stopping short of outlining the slug.
The fine mantle seam is nearly invisible, while the leaf has a narrow blue slit. First I will test one short seven-pixel wet light on the mantle, alone.
The isolated light is short and visible close up, subdued at whole view. I will keep its size, close the leaf slit, and place one small breathing pore on the mantle.
The leaf slit closed and the pore is a small dark mark. I will break the horizontal ground bands with two oblique watery veils and soften the bark ends.
The oblique veils interrupt bands but leave pale vertical starts. Bark end covers changed color more than relief. I will add two unequal mantle spots and reconnect the fern base.
Direct head review: checking the joined roots and unequal feeler turns before correction.
Direct head review shows joined roots and four unequal feelers; the upper root is bulbous. I will narrow that root with a small ground cover and warm the head plane.
The root cover reduced the bulb but left a cool interruption in the feeler. I will restore that narrow join, then make the tail flank turn more softly into the underside.
The tail flank is warmer but its new endpoint is blunt. I will taper that endpoint, then use a faint broken trail and two bark grain marks to suggest dampness.
The thin bark grain is more visible than the trail, and the tail tip stays somewhat blunt. I will quiet one bright grain line and give the fallen leaf a short stem and two veins.

The warm bark cover scarcely reduced the bright line; I will leave that texture. The leaf stem connects. Four long, low moss shoots can tie the empty foreground to the log without competing with the slug.
The foreground shoots stay low and quiet. The fern still has a detached upper-right leaflet and thin lower joins; I will reconnect those areas with broad tapered passes.
The fern upper join now connects. I will give the mantle a few unequal muted spots and restore its small pore after the broad covers, keeping the light separate.
Muted spots are clearer close up than at whole view. I will seat the fallen leaf with a short contact shadow and join the bark light into a broader plane instead of a thin stripe.
The broader bark mark became a light patch; the leaf contact is quiet. I will cover the remaining pale top edge with long wet passes and soften the ground around the leaf.
The top linen edge is covered; long horizontal wash bands remain. I will soften the broad light bark patch, add two unequal moss tips, and warm the shadow-facing mantle edge.
The mantle edge cover left a pale ledge, and the bark patch remains raised. I will soften the ledge with a broader flank plane and give the head two short turns that preserve its feeler joins.
The broad flank softened the ledge only partly; raised seams remain. Final refinement will restore the compact mantle light, join one fern tip, round the leaf shoulder, and close the short head turn.

Finished at 112 marks. The gold body stays joined, feelers unequal, and the restored mantle light compact. The leaf slit and fern upper gap were closed. Blunt tail, ribbon leaflets, raised flank and bark patches, regular ridges and wash bands remain. I will stop: further covers are likely to enlarge those patches rather than improve the light structure.
